title: Supreme Court to weigh fast-track SIR appeals for six more Bengal towns facing civic polls
dek: About 2 lakh deleted voters in Kolkata and six other corporations are waiting on tribunals. The bench said passport holders should be restored quickly and pointed petitioners to the High Court over police checks.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Supreme Court on Friday agreed to consider extending its order for priority hearing of appeals by voters struck off Bengal's rolls, which now covers only the Kolkata Municipal Corporation, to six more municipal bodies where civic elections are due: Howrah, Bally, Haldia, Dhupguri, Kalimpong and Kurseong.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana heard the plea. Justice Bagchi remarked that many deleted voters in the Kolkata area hold valid passports and that tribunals need not take long over such cases, according to reports from the hearing. On complaints that state police were visiting appellants' homes to demand documents, the bench said the petitioners could go to the Calcutta High Court or file a separate petition.

## What was argued

Advocate Prashant Bhushan, for the petitioners, said the court's 23 November order named only the Kolkata corporation, although six others were in the same position. He said about 1.3 lakh appeals were pending in Kolkata and about 75,000 in the other six, roughly two lakh in all, according to reports. He asked that appeals seeking restoration of names be heard separately from appeals challenging the inclusion of other people's names, and suggested that deleted voters whose appeals were still pending on polling day be allowed to vote.

Justice Bagchi said: "It is a difficult task for the tribunals," warning that piling on more urgent matters could make the exercise unrealistic. "We understand the concern. You have made the application; we'll consider it," he said, according to reports. He said restoring eligible voters ahead of the civic polls was the court's "primary concern", and that tribunals could decide the appeals within 30 days. The Chief Justice said the first concern was making sure the appeals were decided.

Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan told the bench that state police had been visiting the homes of appellants with a checklist of documents and asking for identity records by 29 November, and handed the judges a copy. He said the Election Commission had told the petitioners it had nothing to do with the exercise. The Chief Justice asked whether the visits were linked to the pending appeals, and Justice Bagchi asked whether the documents were being placed before the tribunals. Mr Sankaranarayanan said the petitioners would approach the High Court.

The state government's response in court was not reported. Opposition parties have called the police visits intimidation; the BJP, which governs the state, has said they concern law and order and internal security.

## Background

Bengal's special intensive revision of the electoral rolls ahead of this year's Assembly election led to large numbers of deletions. In March the Election Commission set up 19 appellate tribunals on the Supreme Court's direction, and about 700 judicial officers from West Bengal, Odisha and Jharkhand were deployed to deal with roughly 60 lakh claims and objections, according to reports. In its 23 November order, after consulting the Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court, the bench asked the Commission to add tribunals and told them to give priority to appeals against deletion, especially in areas due to vote in civic polls.

## What happens next

The court did not announce when it would rule on the plea for the six other bodies. The police deadline of 29 November for documents falls on Sunday. Dates for the Kolkata and other municipal elections have not yet been announced.
